posture.general_guide: Every project here is a general guide and a starting point. Steps get skipped, reordered, and rewritten in real life. Edit freely.
posture.record_only: These templates organize paperwork and phone calls. They are not legal, financial, or medical advice.
posture.state_variance: Details vary by state. Treat this as the general shape, not the rule where you live.

templates.name: Medicaid application for long term care
templates.subtitle: Applying for coverage of nursing home or facility care

roles.label: Elder law attorney, if you use one

steps: Find out which program you are applying to and get the right form
Write down the local office address, phone, and hours
Gather identification and proof of where they live
Gather proof of all income
Gather bank statements going back as far as the state asks
Gather property, insurance, and burial arrangement papers
Write down anything that was sold, given away, or transferred, and when
Submit the application and note the date you submitted it
Get a case number and write it down
Get the assigned caseworker's name and direct number
Answer every request for more documents and log the date you sent each one
Ask what the decision deadline is and write it down
If it is denied, write down the appeal deadline immediately
Keep a copy of everything you send and everything you receive
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on a caseworker to be assigned
Waiting on a document request to be satisfied
Waiting on a bank for older statements
failure_points: One missing bank statement stalls everything
Transfers nobody remembers making
A document request that arrives while you are away
templates.timeline_shape: Often a few months. Longer whenever a document is missing.

templates.name: Medicaid waiver for care at home
templates.subtitle: Applying for services that let someone stay out of a facility

roles.label: Person who does the needs assessment
Managed care contact, if there is one
Elder law attorney, if you use one

steps: Find out which waiver programs exist where you live
Ask which one fits the situation and write down the name
Ask what the needs assessment involves and who does it
Ask what the financial requirements are
Gather the documents they ask for
Find the local contact and write down the phone and address
Submit the application and note the date
Ask directly whether there is a waiting list
If there is a list, get your placement date in writing and ask about priority categories
Get a case number and the caseworker's direct number
Ask how you will be notified when a spot opens
Answer every document request and log the date
Ask how often you need to confirm you are still waiting
Note the reassessment schedule once services start
documents: Notice that a spot is available
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on the needs assessment to be scheduled
Waiting on a waiting list placement letter
Waiting on a spot to open
Waiting on a caseworker to return a call
failure_points: Sitting on a waiting list with no updates for months
Not knowing whether you are still on the list
Missing the notice when a spot finally opens
templates.timeline_shape: The application takes weeks to months. The waiting list can take much longer, sometimes years in some states.

templates.name: Appeal when Medicare coverage is ending
templates.subtitle: Challenging a discharge or the end of covered services

roles.label: Your regional Medicare quality review organization
Case manager at the hospital or facility

steps: Find the written notice and read it all the way through
Write down which notice it is and the date you received it
Write down the deadline on the notice, exactly as it appears
Call the review organization listed on the notice before the deadline
Ask for the detailed notice that explains the reason
Ask the treating doctor whether they will support continued care in writing
Gather any records that show what care is still needed
Write down that coverage does not require improvement, only a need for skilled care
Note the date and time of every call and who you spoke with
Write down the reference number for the appeal
Ask when a decision will come and how it will arrive
If it is denied, ask what the next level of appeal is and the deadline
Keep copies of every notice and every submission
documents: The detailed notice explaining the reason
A letter from the doctor if you got one
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on a letter from the doctor
failure_points: The deadline is often within a day, so a weekend can cost the appeal
Being told coverage ends because there is no improvement, which is not the standard
Not asking for the detailed notice
templates.timeline_shape: Very fast. Deadlines are often measured in hours, and decisions come within a day or two.

templates.name: Appeal an insurance denial
templates.subtitle: When insurance refuses to approve or pay for something

roles.label: Office of the doctor who ordered it
Employer benefits contact, if it is a work plan

steps: Get the denial letter and find the stated reason
Write down the appeal deadline
Call member services and ask them to explain the process step by step
Ask for the written criteria they used to decide
Ask the ordering doctor's office to write a letter explaining why it is needed
Gather supporting records
Submit the appeal in writing and keep proof of sending
Get a reference number
Log every call with the date, time, and name
Ask when the decision is due
If it is denied again, ask about an outside review and the deadline
Keep copies of everything
failure_points: Missing the appeal window
Never getting the letter from the doctor
Stopping after the first denial instead of asking for outside review
templates.timeline_shape: Usually weeks. Faster if the situation is urgent and you say so.

templates.name: Planning a discharge home
templates.subtitle: Getting ready before someone leaves the hospital or facility

roles.label: Your regional Medicare quality review organization

steps: Write down who to call with questions after discharge
Ask where care happens next and what the options are
Ask what equipment is needed and who orders and delivers it
Ask what help will be needed with daily activities, and be honest about what you can do
Ask for a demonstration of anything you will have to do yourself
Ask the social worker about cost and coverage questions
Ask for the written discharge instructions before you leave
Ask for a written summary of the current condition and medications
Check the medication list against what they were taking before
Write down every follow up appointment and who makes them
Ask what problems to watch for and exactly who to call about each
Write down who to contact if the discharge feels too soon
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on home health to be arranged
Waiting on a follow up appointment to be scheduled
failure_points: Discharge happens before the equipment arrives
Nobody says who makes the follow up appointments
The medication list changed and nobody explained why
templates.timeline_shape: Compressed. You often get a day or two of notice.

templates.name: Requesting medical records
templates.subtitle: Getting copies of records you have a right to see

roles.label: Facility administrator, if you get stuck
Federal health privacy office, for complaints

steps: Figure out exactly who holds the records you want
Ask for their records request form and their process
Confirm what proof they need that you are authorized to request
Write the request down, naming the dates and the records you want
Say what format you want, paper or electronic
Submit it and write down the date you submitted
Ask what the deadline is for them to respond
Ask what the fee is and ask for it in writing
Follow up in writing if the deadline passes
Note you do not have to explain why you want them
If they will not respond, write down the complaint option and the date you filed
Keep a copy of the request, the responses, and everything you receive
failure_points: Being told a patient portal is the only option
Being charged more than copying actually costs
The deadline passing with no answer and no follow up in writing
templates.timeline_shape: Federal rules give them about a month, with one extension allowed if they tell you in writing.
templates.rights_note: Getting a copy of medical records is a federal right under health privacy law, and fees are limited to the cost of copying.

templates.name: Filing a complaint about a facility
templates.subtitle: Going to the ombudsman or the state agency

roles.label: Adult protective services, for suspected abuse

steps: Write down what happened with dates, times, and the names of everyone involved
Decide which route you want: the ombudsman helps resolve, the state agency inspects and enforces
Find the ombudsman contact for your area
Find the state agency contact
Gather your notes, photos, and any records you already have
Ask whether you can file without your name being shared
File the complaint and write down the date
Get a reference number
Ask what priority it was given and what that means for timing
Ask when to expect contact and from whom
Follow up on the date they gave you
Write down the outcome and anything the facility was told to fix
documents: Your written account of what happened
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on a return call from the ombudsman
Waiting on an investigation to be scheduled
Waiting on the facility's correction plan
failure_points: Losing the reference number
A lower priority complaint sitting until the next scheduled inspection
Not writing down names on the day it happened
templates.timeline_shape: Urgent complaints move in days. Others can wait weeks or until the next inspection.

templates.name: Applying for disability benefits
templates.subtitle: A long application with a lot of medical history

roles.label: Disability advocate or attorney, if you use one
Two people who know the situation well

steps: Find out which program applies and get the starter materials
Gather identification and the social security number
List every doctor, clinic, and hospital with dates of treatment
List work history going back as far as they ask
Build the current medication list
Write down two people who can describe the daily situation
Complete the application, online or in person
Submit and write down the date and the claim number
Answer every request for more information and log the dates
Ask when a decision is expected
If it is denied, write down the appeal deadline the same day
Keep copies of everything, including the denial
documents: List of doctors and treatment dates
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on medical records to be sent
Waiting on an appeal hearing date
failure_points: Gaps in the medical history
Missing an appeal deadline after a denial
Incomplete work history
templates.timeline_shape: Months for a first decision. Appeals add more months.

templates.name: Veteran and caregiver benefits
templates.subtitle: Applying for benefits available to veterans and their caregivers
steps: Find out which programs the situation might qualify for
Write down the difference between the ones you are applying to
Confirm what service and disability documentation is needed
Get the right application form for each program
Complete any parts that need both the veteran and the caregiver
Gather service records and disability documentation
Gather medical evidence about the care that is needed
Submit the application and write down the date
Call the support line and confirm it was received
Ask what the review steps are and how long each takes
Complete any in home assessment that is scheduled
Get the decision in writing
If it is denied, ask what review options exist and the deadline
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on an assessment to be scheduled
Waiting on a review after a denial
failure_points: Documenting the caregiving arrangement incorrectly
Submitting only one half of a joint application
Missing the disability rating documentation
templates.timeline_shape: Several months, with multiple review stages.

templates.name: Guardianship or conservatorship
templates.subtitle: A court process for decision making when someone cannot decide

roles.label: Court appointed evaluator or examining doctor

steps: Understand that this is a court process and it works differently in every state
Ask whether a less restrictive option would work instead, like a power of attorney
Find the court's self help resource or information line
Find out which forms are required and where to file
Find out whether an attorney is required where you live
Gather the medical documentation the court requires
Find out who has to be notified and how
File the petition and write down the case number
Write down the hearing date and what to bring
Attend the hearing
Get a copy of the court order
Write down what reports you must file afterward and when they are due
documents: Ongoing reports you have to file
failure_points: Starting a court case when a simpler document would have worked
Missing the reports that are due after appointment
Not knowing who must be notified
templates.timeline_shape: Weeks to months. Much longer if anyone contests it.
templates.advice_note: This is not legal advice. Guardianship law is different in every state and a lawyer is usually involved.

templates.name: Setting up legal and medical decision papers
templates.subtitle: Power of attorney, health care decision maker, and written wishes

roles.label: The person being named to decide

steps: Learn which documents exist and what each one does
Note that money decisions and medical decisions are usually separate documents
Note that written wishes are planning, while signed medical orders are followed by responders
Decide who will be named, and name a backup
Get the forms that are valid in your state
Complete them while the person can still make their own decisions
Sign with whatever witnesses or notary your state requires
Give copies to the named person, the doctors, and the facility
Write down where every original is kept, specifically
Ask the doctor about signed medical orders if the situation is serious
Put all of it on the emergency card
Review after any major change in health
documents: A note of where each original is kept
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on the doctor to sign medical orders
Waiting on copies to reach the facility
failure_points: Signed incorrectly for your state and not valid
Nobody has a copy when it is needed
Confusing written wishes with orders that responders can follow
templates.timeline_shape: Can be done in a week. Signed medical orders need a doctor.
templates.advice_note: This is not legal advice. What these documents are called and how they must be signed varies by state.
templates.localization_note: Do not translate these document names with direct cognates. Use descriptive wording plus a plain explanation in each language.

templates.name: Taking leave from work to provide care
templates.subtitle: Requesting protected time off for yourself

roles.label: The doctor who will complete the form
Federal labor department, if there is a problem

steps: Check whether your employer and your own work history qualify
Tell your employer you need time off to care for a family member
Give as much notice as you can, in writing
Ask human resources for the paperwork
Get the medical certification form to the doctor's office quickly
Note the deadline for returning the certification
Keep the notices your employer gives you
Ask whether the leave is paid, unpaid, or can be combined with paid time
Ask how the leave gets tracked if you take it a few hours at a time
Keep your own log of every hour used
Confirm in writing what was approved and for how long
Ask what happens when the leave runs out
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on the paperwork from human resources
Waiting on the doctor to complete the form
failure_points: The certification arrives late and the leave is denied
Nobody tracks the hours taken a little at a time
Assuming it is paid when it is not
templates.timeline_shape: Days to a few weeks, mostly waiting on forms.

templates.name: Moving to a different facility
templates.subtitle: Arranging a transfer from one place to another

roles.label: Case manager where they are now

steps: Write down the reason for the move and what you want instead
Confirm the new place has a bed and accepts the coverage
Ask the current case manager to start the transfer
Confirm who sends the records and the medication list
Confirm the medication list actually arrives, do not assume
Arrange transport and confirm the time
Ask whether the current bed is held and for how long
Confirm coverage or authorization for the new place
Get the transfer date in writing
Write down the new room number, floor, and direct phone
Rebuild the contact list for the new place
Keep copies of the transfer paperwork
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on a bed to open
failure_points: Records and medication lists that never arrive
Losing the old bed before the new one is confirmed
A coverage gap between the two places
templates.timeline_shape: Days to weeks, depending on beds and approvals.

templates.name: Fighting a facility discharge
templates.subtitle: When a facility says someone has to leave

roles.label: State office that handles these appeals

steps: Get the notice in writing and read it carefully
Check that it states a reason, where they are supposed to go, and how to appeal
Write down the date on the notice and the date you received it
Note that federal rules allow facility initiated discharge only for a short list of reasons
Note that a notice of only a day or two is almost never proper
Call the ombudsman the same day
File the appeal by the deadline on the notice
Ask whether they can stay while the appeal is decided
Gather payment records and care records
Write down every conversation with the facility, with names and times
Prepare for the hearing and ask the ombudsman what to expect
If they are in the hospital, ask about the right to come back to their bed
Keep copies of everything
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on a call back from the ombudsman
Waiting on written confirmation they can stay
failure_points: Very short notice that nobody challenges
Confusing coverage ending with being evicted, they are different things
Being refused readmission after a hospital stay
templates.timeline_shape: Fast. The appeal usually has to be filed before the discharge date on the notice.
templates.rights_note: Federal rules for nursing homes limit why a facility can discharge someone, generally require advance written notice, and give a right to appeal.
templates.advice_note: This is not legal advice. Call the ombudsman early, they do this for free.

templates.name: Documenting money for a Medicaid application
templates.subtitle: Organizing years of financial records

roles.label: Elder law attorney or Medicaid planner

steps: Ask exactly how many years of records the state wants
Request statements from every bank and account for that whole period
List every account, property, policy, and vehicle
Write down anything that was sold, gifted, or moved, with dates
Keep receipts for medical bills that were paid
Keep receipts for home changes and repairs
Keep any prepaid funeral or burial paperwork
Organize everything by year and by account
Ask the caseworker what counts and what does not where you live
Consider a consultation with someone who does this professionally
Submit the documentation together, not piece by piece
Keep a copy of everything you handed over
documents: Bank statements for the full lookback period
waiting_on_prompts: Waiting on the caseworker to confirm what is missing
failure_points: A transfer nobody can explain, which can cause a penalty period
Statements the bank charges for or takes weeks to produce
Assuming something is exempt when it is not
templates.timeline_shape: Runs alongside the application. Gathering old statements is usually the slow part.
templates.advice_note: This is not legal or financial advice. Rules vary by state and mistakes here have real consequences.

templates.name: Sorting out bills and insurance statements
templates.subtitle: Matching what was billed against what was covered

roles.label: Billing office where the care happened

steps: Collect every bill and every insurance statement in one place
Match each bill to the statement that covers the same visit
Write down what insurance paid and what is actually owed
Flag anything where the two do not match
Do not pay a bill before the insurance statement arrives
Call the billing office about anything unclear and log the call
Call insurance if the statement looks wrong
Ask for a corrected statement or bill in writing
Open a dispute if it is not resolved and get a reference number
Write down the payment deadline so a dispute does not become a late payment
Ask whether a payment plan is available if the balance is real
Keep copies of everything
failure_points: Paying before the statement arrives
A disputed bill going to collections while you wait
Bills from providers you never chose
